title: Total Area Through an Interface
statement:
An interface is a promise that every implementing type keeps in its own
way: ask any `IShape` for its `Area()`, and it answers correctly, without
the code asking having to know or care *which* shape it is holding. That
is the entire point of polymorphism -- and the easiest way to lose it by
accident is to write code that checks the concrete type anyway.

## The interface

```
public interface IShape
{
    double Area();
}
```

Two implementations are already provided:

```
public class Circle : IShape       // Area() = π × Radius²
public class Rectangle : IShape    // Area() = Width × Height
```

## Your function

```
public static double TotalArea(List<IShape> shapes);
```

Return the sum of `Area()` across every shape in `shapes`. `shapes` may be
empty, in which case the total is `0`.

## Watch out

- **`shapes` is not guaranteed to hold only `Circle` and `Rectangle`.**
  Any type implementing `IShape` is a legal element -- including ones this
  statement never names. Code that pattern-matches on `is Circle` /
  `is Rectangle` and falls through to a default for anything else silently
  gets the wrong answer (typically `0`, or a thrown exception) for a shape
  it was never told the identity of, when calling `Area()` directly would
  have worked without needing to know.
- **`shapes.Sum(s => s.Area())` and a plain loop that adds `shape.Area()`
  into a running total are the same operation** -- pick whichever reads
  more clearly to you; the correctness question here is not about the
  looping construct, it is about calling `Area()` through the interface at
  all rather than routing around it.

tests.name: an empty list totals to zero
a circle and a rectangle together
an undocumented third shape must still be handled correctly
tests.description: 0.5 * 6 * 4 = 12 -- code that only recognises Circle and Rectangle has no branch for this and gets it wrong; shape.Area() does not need to be told.

tests.name: all three kinds mixed in one list
